column4: The section reads human life as successive states; لَتَرْكَبُنَّ طَبَقًا عَن طَبَقٍ directly presents passage from stage to stage.
After 84:19's successive states and the intervening denial, this ayah repeats the section's exact outcome for believers who do good: أَجْرٌ غَيْرُ مَمْنُونٍ.
This is the section's fullest stated parallel: dust, drop, clot, formed and unformed flesh, childhood, maturity, senescence, death, revived earth, and resurrection all occupy one evidentiary arc.
The ayah lays out dust, drop, clot, childhood, full strength, old age, earlier death, and an appointed term, matching the section's entire ascent and decline.
Weakness, strength, then weakness and gray hair give the same temporal contour as best bodily completion followed by reversal.
نُنَكِّسْهُ فِى ٱلْخَلْقِ makes long life an inversion within creation, the section's precise reading of being returned downward in old age.
The ayah says some are يُرَدُّ إِلَىٰ أَرْذَلِ ٱلْعُمُرِ until knowledge is lost, directly identifying the section's return with senescence.
The section hears ṭawr, “stage,” behind ṭūr; this ayah directly says God created people أَطْوَارًا, in successive stages.
خَلْقًا مِّنۢ بَعْدِ خَلْقٍ in three womb-darknesses supplies the section's exact creation-after-creation formulation.
The clot, morsel, bones, flesh, and emergence as another creation enact form becoming complete; أَحْسَنُ ٱلْخَٰلِقِينَ also joins creation to “best.”
After the formative sequence of 23:12–14, this ayah marks the certain cutoff of those stages in death.
This ayah completes the preceding creation-and-death sequence with resurrection on the Day of Judgment, answering the section's final challenge to denial.
خَلَقَكَ فَسَوَّىٰكَ فَعَدَلَكَ names creation, proportioning, and bodily adjustment together, directly paralleling completed form and best stature.
فِىٓ أَىِّ صُورَةٍۢ مَّا شَآءَ رَكَّبَكَ makes the human form a divinely composed configuration, clarifying the section's concern with changing form.
After 82:7–8 describe bodily formation, كَلَّا بَلْ تُكَذِّبُونَ بِٱلدِّينِ makes denial of Judgment the same startling response challenged in 95:7.
The ayah places the human at the emitted-drop stage, opening the same formation sequence that the section follows toward complete stature.
The clot is then خَلَقَ فَسَوَّىٰ, created and proportioned, directly expressing the section's completion of form.
After the embryonic sequence, the question whether its Maker can revive the dead reproduces the section's move from visible life stages to Judgment.
مِن نُّطْفَةٍ خَلَقَهُۥ فَقَدَّرَهُۥ joins creation from a drop to exact determination, a concise parallel to formation and bodily measure.
Within the ordered sequence begun at 80:18, this ayah makes death and burial the end of the earthly span.
ثُمَّ إِذَا شَآءَ أَنشَرَهُۥ carries the same ordered sequence beyond death into resurrection.
The rhetorical أَلَمْ نَخْلُقكُّم مِّن مَّآءٍۢ مَّهِينٍۢ begins an argument from the reader's own earliest stage.
The lowly fluid is placed in a secure womb, locating the first stage before bodily form appears.
إِلَىٰ قَدَرٍۢ مَّعْلُومٍۢ gives gestation a known measure and endpoint, matching the section's staged timeline.
فَقَدَرْنَا declares divine measuring after the womb sequence and turns it into an appeal to recognize the One who forms.
The warning to deniers immediately after 77:20–23 parallels the section's question of how Judgment can still be denied after human formation is displayed.
نَحْنُ خَلَقْنَٰكُمْ فَلَوْلَا تُصَدِّقُونَ couples human creation with a rebuke for failing to affirm, closely matching the section's final stance.
The question whether humans create the emitted seed or God does identifies the true agent of the first bodily stage.
نَحْنُ قَدَّرْنَا بَيْنَكُمُ ٱلْمَوْتَ makes death a measured terminus within the creation sequence.
Replacing human likenesses and originating people in an unknown form extends the section's change of form beyond senescence.
Knowledge of the first origination is made the reason to remember, exactly the section's argument from life's seen stages to what follows.
أَحْسَنَ كُلَّ شَىْءٍ خَلَقَهُۥ joins “best” with creation and begins human creation from clay, closely echoing best created form.
The descendant is then made from an extract of lowly fluid, supplying the next human stage in the local sequence.
ثُمَّ سَوَّىٰهُ describes the human as proportioned before receiving faculties, matching form's completion at the section's summit.
After 32:7–9 recount creation and proportioning, the objection to being a new creation when lost in earth enacts the very denial the section finds unreasonable.
The believer asks whether his companion rejects the One who made him from dust, then a drop, then سَوَّىٰكَ رَجُلًا, a fully formed man.
A human created from a drop becomes an open disputant; the sudden span from origin to denial mirrors the section's rebuke after displaying a lifetime.
The denier forgets his own creation and asks who can revive decayed bones, concretizing the section's point that created form wears away.
The answer is that the One who originated the bones the first time will revive them, turning first creation into evidence for return.
The human asks incredulously whether he will be brought out alive after death, voicing the denial at the end of the section's timeline.
The reply recalls that God created the human before he was anything, using the first beginning to answer the preceding resurrection doubt.
ٱلْخَلْقِ ٱلْأَوَّلِ is set against doubt about خَلْقٍۢ جَدِيدٍۢ, making first creation the direct proof of renewed creation.
Creation from earth, return into it, and emergence another time state the full outward-and-back arc that the section's stages imply.
The rebuke “How can you disbelieve?” is followed by lifelessness, life, death, renewed life, and return to God, an exact argumentative lifecycle.
God creates, provides, causes death, and gives life; the four acts place the finite human span inside divine origination and renewal.
The question asks whether people see how God begins creation and then repeats it, matching the section's appeal to visible creation as evidence.
Observation of how creation began leads explicitly to ٱلنَّشْأَةَ ٱلْـَٔاخِرَةَ, completing the first-life-to-next-life inference.
Dust, drop, pairing, womb knowledge, long life, and life shortened are all held in a record, directly joining formation to measured lifespan.
The ayah reaches behind formed life to a stretch of time when the human was not yet a thing mentioned, marking the zero point of the section's stages.
Creation from a mixed drop proceeds to hearing and sight for a test, showing faculties emerging from an unformed beginning.
صَوَّرَكُمْ فَأَحْسَنَ صُوَرَكُمْ joins bestowed human form, its excellence, and final return in one ayah.
صَوَّرَكُمْ فَأَحْسَنَ صُوَرَكُمْ directly states that God formed people and made their forms beautiful, clarifying “best stature” as completed embodiment.
God forms people in wombs however He wills, directly locating the section's appearance of form within gestation.
ٱلَّذِى خَلَقَ فَسَوَّىٰ compresses creation and proportioning into the same pairing used in the detailed human-stage passages.
Believers who do good receive أَجْرٌ غَيْرُ مَمْنُونٍ, the section's exact claim that reward continues when bodily stages end.
أَجْرًا غَيْرَ مَمْنُونٍ repeats the uncut reward formula; its singular addressee shows the phrase's promise beyond the general believer formula.
The section's dictionary noun al-manūn names death because it cuts duration; رَيْبَ ٱلْمَنُونِ is precisely the death or fatal turn the opponents await.
The oath by time directly frames the chronological reading that the section develops from the human body's successive states.
After the oath by time, the human is declared to be in loss, giving a compressed counterpart to created strength passing into decline.
The exception for faith and righteous deeds matches 95:6 and identifies what escapes the loss announced over time.
Immediately after “stage after stage,” the question why they do not believe supplies the same astonished stance as 95:7.
بَلِ ٱلَّذِينَ كَفَرُوا۟ يُكَذِّبُونَ names denial after the sequence of stages, preparing the identical exception and reward in 84:25.
The question whether the human expects to be left without purpose opens a sequence that answers through his bodily origin and resurrection.
The male and female are made from the preceding embryonic stages, marking differentiation within completed human formation.
The rebuke of human ingratitude begins the birth-to-resurrection sequence, giving the section's final challenge a close rhetorical counterpart.
The question “From what did He create him?” directs attention to the bodily beginning before 80:19 supplies the drop and measure.
After creation and measuring, ثُمَّ ٱلسَّبِيلَ يَسَّرَهُۥ places the lived course between formation and death.
The question what deluded the human concerning his generous Lord opens the formation-to-denial sequence and parallels the section's closing interrogation.
Human creation from an extract of clay begins the ordered stages that culminate in another creation at 23:14.
Placement as a drop in a secure lodging supplies the womb setting between clay-origin and the formed embryo.
Creation from clay and the decree of a term are followed by human doubt, joining bodily origin, bounded lifetime, and denial in one ayah.
Creation from dust followed by people spreading as full humans telescopes the rise from material beginning to mature embodied life.
Creation from an emitted drop provides the bodily beginning immediately before the passage asserts the later origination.
وَأَنَّ عَلَيْهِ ٱلنَّشْأَةَ ٱلْأُخْرَىٰ makes the second origination belong to the same Creator who produced the drop-stage.
The command that the human look at what he was created from adopts the section's method of making bodily origin an argument.
Creation from gushing fluid states the earliest material stage in that argument.
After identifying human origin, the ayah declares God able to return him, moving from first formation to return.
The humbled earth trembles and swells with water, and its reviver is declared able to revive the dead; this is the exact secondary earth-scene noted from 22:5.
The command to observe earth revived after death ends by affirming that the same One revives the dead, repeating the section's evidentiary analogy.
Rain revives a dead land and the ayah concludes كَذَٰلِكَ ٱلنُّشُورُ, making seasonal revival a model of human rising.
Measured rain revives a dead land and كَذَٰلِكَ تُخْرَجُونَ explicitly maps that scene onto human emergence.
Rain gives life to a dead land and كَذَٰلِكَ ٱلْخُرُوجُ identifies it with resurrection, matching the secondary proof inside 22:5.
Heavy clouds are driven to dead land, fruit emerges, and the ayah says the dead are brought out likewise.
Bringing living from dead, dead from living, and reviving earth culminate in the promise that humans will be brought out in the same way.
What people possess runs out while what is with God remains, followed by promised reward; this states the section's finite-life versus uncut-reward relation.
Every soul tastes death, but full recompense comes on Resurrection Day; bodily duration ends before reward is delivered.
Gestation and weaning, attainment of full strength, and the age of forty make a measured human timeline whose mature response is gratitude and good action.
Death and life are created as a test of who is best in deed, joining the cut lifespan to the moral outcome that survives it.
عَطَآءً غَيْرَ مَجْذُوذٍ describes Paradise's gift as uncut, a direct semantic parallel to the section's reward that is not severed.
Humans leave the womb knowing nothing and receive hearing, sight, and hearts; beside 16:70's old-age loss of knowledge, this makes life's cognitive arc return toward its beginning.
عَلَّمَ ٱلْإِنسَٰنَ مَا لَمْ يَعْلَمْ marks knowledge gained after initial ignorance, the reverse edge of the section's senile “knows nothing after knowledge.”

The section's dictionary sense of gh-y-r is change of form without change of self; Satan's command فَلَيُغَيِّرُنَّ خَلْقَ ٱللَّهِ gives a culpable, deliberate alteration of creation against involuntary aging.
Preferring the nearer life fixes desire on the passing side of the section's finite-life and enduring-reward boundary.
The Hereafter is خَيْرٌ وَأَبْقَىٰ, supplying the enduring side that outlasts bodily stages.
Every being on earth is passing away, universalizing the section's claim that created form wears out.
The enduring face of the majestic Lord remains when created beings pass, sharpening the boundary between finite creation and what does not end.
خُلِقَ ٱلْإِنسَٰنُ ضَعِيفًا states created human weakness; it bounds “best stature” by recalling the weakness from which strength rises and to which age returns.
Zechariah's weakened bones and head blazing with gray hair make the bodily wearing of old age visible from within a single person.
The deniers ask whether they will be مَرْدُودُونَ to the former state; the section's downward return in age is set beside the denied return after death.
Their objection points to decayed bones, making worn created matter the boundary they wrongly treat as preventing restoration.
Bones and crumbled remains are invoked against becoming a new creation, turning the body's wearing away into a denial of the next stage.
The command to become stone or iron intensifies the imagined barrier of bodily material rather than conceding that decay defeats return.
The answer “the One who originated you the first time” makes first formation overcome even the hardest imagined form.
Worldly life and a plant both pass through attraction, growth, yellowing, and debris, while the ayah sets that wearing cycle against the Hereafter.
The parable of worldly life moves from rain-fed mingling growth to dry fragments scattered by wind, a natural image of formed life wearing out.
Worldly adornments are set against enduring righteous deeds and their better reward, matching the section's reward beyond the body's decline.
Rain-fed plants vary in color, wither, yellow, and become debris; their visible stages parallel bodily rise and deterioration.
Worldly provision and adornment are temporary, while what is with God is better and more lasting, restating the finite-versus-enduring boundary.
Worldly goods are temporary enjoyment, whereas what is with God is better and more lasting for believers, aligning duration with faith.
Nuh asks why his people do not accord God due majesty; 71:14 supplies their staged creation as the reason, paralleling the section's rebuke after the stages are shown.
The human is laboring onward to the Lord and will meet Him, compressing an earthly course and its final encounter into one address.
Divine measuring and guidance follow creation and proportioning in 87:2, giving ordered fitness to the formed creature.
خَلَقَ ٱلْإِنسَٰنَ مِنْ عَلَقٍ names the clot-stage alone, a concise occurrence of the formative sequence developed at length elsewhere.
When Joseph reaches full maturity, he receives judgment and knowledge; this supplies a concrete middle peak between newborn ignorance and old-age forgetting.
Moses receives judgment and knowledge upon reaching full strength and maturity, again marking the section's summit as a life stage with new capacity.
The death people flee will meet them and they will then be returned for disclosure of their deeds, joining life's cutoff to judgment.
No soul is delayed once its appointed term arrives, specifying the irreversible cutoff implied by the section's al-manūn gloss.
God takes souls at death and during sleep, retains the one decreed to die, and releases the other until a named term, making duration and its cutoff explicit.
The parable of worldly life races from rain-fed abundance to sudden removal as though it had not flourished, another visible arc from formation to disappearance.
God brings out pasture, beginning a compact created-life sequence that ends in withered matter in the next ayah.
The pasture is made dark stubble, an elemental analogue for created form passing from fullness to worn remains.
وَٱلطُّورِ is another oath by the Mount; it confirms that Qur'anic ṭūr names the mountain even though the section deliberately hears the homophonous “stage.”
The tree growing from طُورِ سَيْنَآءَ anchors ṭūr as Sinai and even joins the Mount to the olive, clarifying that the life-stage link is phonetic rather than the mountain's lexical meaning.
God's call to Moses from the right side of ٱلطُّورِ places the noun in the Sinai encounter, maintaining the semantic boundary from ṭawr, “stage.”
The appointment at the right side of ٱلطُّورِ again fixes the word as the Mount within the exodus story, not a creation stage.
Moses sees a fire from the side of ٱلطُّورِ; the concrete mountain scene distinguishes the source section's sound association from ayah meaning.
The divine call at the side of ٱلطُّورِ identifies the same mountain setting and so guards the section's stated distinction between mountain and stage.
The Mount is raised above Israel at the covenant; this physical action confirms ṭūr's mountain sense against the section's secondary sound-play.
The repeated covenant scene again has the Mount raised overhead, another concrete Qur'anic use of ṭūr as an object rather than a temporal stage.
The Mount raised over the people for their covenant supplies the same distinct mountain sense on which the section's phonetic bridge depends.
God does not يُغَيِّرُ a people's condition until they change what is within themselves; this moral change of state contrasts with bodily form changing through age.
God does not change a bestowed favor until a people change themselves, another volitional use of gh-y-r that bounds the section's involuntary bodily change.
The children of Adam are honored and preferred over much creation, giving a dignity counterpart to the section's best human stature.
God's command to prostrate comes only after the human has been proportioned and ensouled, making completed form a threshold.
As in 15:29, proportioning the human precedes the breathed spirit and angelic prostration, linking completion of form with elevated status.
“We created you, then formed you” distinguishes origination from bestowed shape, the same distinction the section draws around completed form.
The human is created in toil; this qualifies bodily excellence by naming the arduous condition through which the life's stages pass.
The objection that dust and bones cannot be raised treats the worn body's final state as an endpoint, precisely the denial challenged after the section's life course.
The question whether dead dust and bones can be raised repeats the boundary that bodily decay seems to impose but resurrection crosses.
The same dust-and-bones objection appears inside a passage already reasoning from human creation and measured death.
God's revival of earth after death is offered as a clarified sign for understanding, supporting the dry-earth proof explicitly noticed in the section.
A dead earth revived to produce grain offers the same visible movement from lifelessness to productive life, though resurrection is supplied by the surrounding argument.
Rain revives earth after death as a sign for listeners, echoing the secondary field scene in 22:5 without itself explicitly naming human resurrection.
Enduring righteous deeds are better in reward and return, supporting the section's claim that good action yields value beyond the changing life.
The flower of worldly life is a temporary test, while the Lord's provision is better and more lasting, another duration boundary around earthly flourishing.
Paradisal provision is described as having no exhaustion, a concrete semantic parallel to reward that is not cut off.
Paradise fruit is neither cut off nor withheld, giving material shape to the section's unsevered recompense.
The fluid's bodily source continues 86:5–6's origin scene; its anatomical formulation is relevant only as part of that formation-to-return argument, not as a separate life stage.
Every soul tastes death and is then returned to God; this plausibly compresses the cutoff and return, though it does not display the intervening stages.
Every soul tastes death and is returned after testing; the relation to the section is specific to life's endpoint and moral outcome, but the bodily arc is unstated.
